pairs.source_text: superavit aerumnis suis aerumnas Herculi. nam cum leone, cum excetra, cum cervo, cum apro Aetolico, cum avibus Stymphalicis, cum Antaeo deluctari mavelim, quam cum Amore.
pairs.question: Cuius herois labores Toxilus in Persa Plauti suas amoris aerumnas superare gloriatur?
pairs.question_en: Whose labors does Toxilus in Plautus' Persa boast that his own toils of love surpass?
pairs.derivation: Toxilus opens the play claiming his love-toils exceed the labors of Hercules (the lion, the Hydra, the boar, the Stymphalian birds, Antaeus). Anchored to Toxilus + the play; one-name answer supported verbatim (superavit aerumnis suis aerumnas Herculi). Culturally salient myth of Hercules' labors.

pairs.source_text: Profecto domino suos amores Toxilus emit atque curat, leno ut emittat manu;
pairs.question: Quo absente servus Toxilus in Persa Plauti amores suos redimit et totam fallaciam gerit?
pairs.question_en: In whose absence does the slave Toxilus in Plautus' Persa buy his beloved's freedom and run the whole intrigue?
pairs.derivation: The distinctive premise of the Persa: a slave (Toxilus) is himself the lover and the schemer, acting while his master is abroad. Anchored to Toxilus + the play; short answer supported verbatim (Profecto domino... Toxilus emit atque curat). A notable mores-fact of Roman comedy.

pairs.source_text: Vt mihi des nummos sescentos, quos pro capite illius pendam, quos continuo tibi reponam in hoc triduo, aut quadriduo.
pairs.question: Quot nummos Toxilus in Persa Plauti mutuos petit, ut amicam suam pro capite eius redimat?
pairs.question_en: How many coins does Toxilus in Plautus' Persa seek to borrow, to redeem his beloved by paying for her?
pairs.derivation: The sum needed to free Toxilus' beloved: six hundred nummi paid pro capite (for her person). Anchored to Toxilus + the play; single-number answer supported verbatim (nummos sescentos... pro capite illius pendam). Currency and manumission realia.

pairs.source_text: Veterem atque antiquom quaestum maiorum meum servo atque obtineo et magna cum cura colo. nam numquam quisquam meorum maiorum fuit, quin parasitando paverint ventres suos.
pairs.question: Quem quaestum a maioribus hereditarium Saturio in Persa Plauti se tenere gloriatur?
pairs.question_en: What ancestral, hereditary trade does Saturio in Plautus' Persa boast of keeping up?
pairs.answer_en: That of a parasite, earning his keep by sponging.
pairs.derivation: Saturio boasts the parasite's trade is his ancestral profession: none of his forebears ever fed his belly except by sponging. Anchored to Saturio + the play; answer supported verbatim (quaestum maiorum... parasitando paverint ventres suos). The parasite-economy is a culturally salient comic institution.

pairs.source_text: SAT. Pernam quidem ius est adponi frigidam postridie.
pairs.question: Quomodo pernam postridie apponi oportere Saturio parasitus in Persa Plauti dicit?
pairs.question_en: How does the parasite Saturio in Plautus' Persa say ham ought to be served the next day?
pairs.derivation: A point of table lore: ham (perna) is properly served cold the day after. Anchored to Saturio + the play; one-word answer supported verbatim (Pernam... adponi frigidam postridie). Culturally salient food custom.

pairs.source_text: SAT. Memini: ut murena et conger ne calefierent; nam nimio melius oppectuntur frigida.
pairs.question: Quos duos pisces melius frigidos quam calidos comedi Saturio in Persa Plauti affirmat?
pairs.question_en: Which two fish does Saturio in Plautus' Persa say are far better eaten cold than warmed?
pairs.derivation: Gastronomic lore: moray and conger eels are much better eaten cold than reheated. Anchored to Saturio + the play; two-name answer supported verbatim (murena et conger... melius oppectuntur frigida). Culturally salient Roman fish cookery.

pairs.source_text: SAT. Pothen ornamenta? TOX. Abs chorago sumito; dare debet: praebenda aediles locaverunt.
pairs.question: A quo scaenica ornamenta sumi solere Toxilus in Persa Plauti dicit?
pairs.question_en: From whom does Toxilus in Plautus' Persa say stage costumes are usually got?
pairs.derivation: Metatheatrical realia: the choragus supplies the stage costumes, their provision let out by the aediles. Anchored to the play; one-word answer supported verbatim (Abs chorago sumito... praebenda aediles locaverunt). Culturally salient bit of Roman theater production.

pairs.source_text: sed longe ab Athenis esse se gnatam autumet;
pairs.question: In qua urbe fabula Plauti Persa agitur?
pairs.question_en: In which city is Plautus' Persa set?
pairs.derivation: The play is set in Athens: the girl is coached to claim she was born far from Athens, the local reference point. Anchored to the play; one-place answer supported by the text (longe ab Athenis esse se gnatam autumet). Canonical setting of the comedy.

pairs.source_text: nam erus meus me Eretriam misit, domitos boves ut sibi mercarer, dedit argentum, nam ibi mercatum dixit esse die septumi.
pairs.question: Quo Sagaristio a domino suo in Persa Plauti missus est, ut domitos boves emeret?
pairs.question_en: Where was Sagaristio sent by his master in Plautus' Persa to buy broken-in oxen?
pairs.derivation: Sagaristio's master sent him to Eretria with money to buy oxen at the market there; he diverts the money to help Toxilus. Anchored to Sagaristio + the play; one-place answer supported verbatim (erus meus me Eretriam misit, domitos boves ut sibi mercarer).

pairs.source_text: Iovi opulento, incluto, Ope gnato, supremo, valido, viripotenti,
pairs.question: Cuius deae filium Sagaristio Iovem in Persa Plauti appellat?
pairs.question_en: Of which goddess does Sagaristio in Plautus' Persa call Jupiter the son?
pairs.derivation: Roman theogony: Jupiter is styled Ope gnatus, son of the goddess Ops. Anchored to the play; one-name answer supported verbatim (Iovi... Ope gnato). Culturally salient divine genealogy.

pairs.source_text: librorum eccillum habeo plenum soracum. si hoc adcurassis lepide, cui rei operam damus, dabuntur dotis tibi inde sescenti logi, atque Attici omnes; nullum Siculum acceperis.
pairs.question: Quam dotem Saturio parasitus filiae suae in Persa Plauti pollicetur?
pairs.answer: Sescentos logos (iocos) Atticos ex soraco librorum suorum.
pairs.question_en: What dowry does the parasite Saturio promise his daughter in Plautus' Persa?
pairs.answer_en: Six hundred jokes, all Attic, from his hamper full of books.
pairs.derivation: The parasite's stock-in-trade: a hamper (soracus) full of joke-books, whence he offers six hundred jokes (logi) as dowry, all Attic and no Sicilian. Anchored to Saturio + the play; answer supported verbatim (dotis tibi inde sescenti logi, atque Attici omnes). The ridicularia are a culturally salient feature of the parasite's economy.

pairs.source_text: et istas tabellas, quas consignavi tibi, quas tu attulisti mi ab ero meo usque e Persia.
pairs.question: Vnde Sagaristio in Persa Plauti se epistulam attulisse simulat, ut Dordalum lenonem decipiat?
pairs.question_en: From where does Sagaristio in Plautus' Persa pretend to have brought a letter, to deceive the pimp Dordalus?
pairs.derivation: The title-trick: Sagaristio poses as a messenger bearing a letter all the way from Persia. Anchored to Sagaristio + the play; one-place answer supported verbatim (attulisti mi ab ero meo usque e Persia). The Persian sham gives the comedy its name.

pairs.source_text: TOX. Euge, euge, exornatu's basilice; tiara ornatum lepida condecorat schema.
pairs.question: Quo capitis ornamento Sagaristio ornatus est, ut Persam simulet in Persa Plauti?
pairs.question_en: With what headdress is Sagaristio adorned to play the Persian in Plautus' Persa?
pairs.derivation: The Persian disguise is marked by the tiara, the oriental headdress. Anchored to Sagaristio + the play; one-word answer supported verbatim (tiara ornatum lepida condecorat schema). Culturally salient marker of the Persian.

pairs.source_text: Salutem dicit Toxilo Timarchides et familiae omni.
pairs.question: Quod nomen habet dominus Toxili, a quo epistula ficta in Persa Plauti mitti fingitur?
pairs.question_en: What is the name of Toxilus' master, from whom the forged letter is pretended to be sent in Plautus' Persa?
pairs.derivation: The sham letter is headed as from Toxilus' master, Timarchides. Anchored to Toxilus + the play; one-name answer supported verbatim (Salutem dicit Toxilo Timarchides).

pairs.source_text: Chrysopolim Persae cepere urbem in Arabia, plenam bonarum rerum atque antiquom oppidum.
pairs.question: Quam urbem, in Arabia sitam, Persae in epistula ficta Persae Plauti cepisse dicuntur?
pairs.question_en: What city, situated in Arabia, are the Persians said to have captured in the forged letter of Plautus' Persa?
pairs.derivation: The mock-Persian exotica of the sham letter: the Persians have taken Chrysopolis, a rich old city 'in Arabia,' whose booty is being auctioned. Anchored to the play; one-place answer supported verbatim (Chrysopolim Persae cepere urbem in Arabia). The fabricated geography that props up the trick.

pairs.source_text: Iste qui tabellas adfert adduxit simul forma expetenda liberalem virginem, furtivam, abductam ex Arabia penitissuma.
pairs.question: Vnde abducta esse fingitur virgo captiva quam Sagaristio Dordalo in Persa Plauti vendit?
pairs.question_en: From where is the captive maiden, whom Sagaristio sells to Dordalus in Plautus' Persa, pretended to have been carried off?
pairs.derivation: The disguised girl is passed off as a stolen freeborn maiden brought from the depths of Arabia. Anchored to the play; short answer supported verbatim (furtivam, abductam ex Arabia penitissuma). Part of the exotic sham.

pairs.source_text: ac suo periclo is emat qui eam mercabitur: mancipio neque promittet neque quisquam dabit.
pairs.question: Qua condicione virgo captiva Dordalo in Persa Plauti venditur, cum eam nemo mancipio daturus sit?
pairs.question_en: On what terms is the captive maiden sold to Dordalus in Plautus' Persa, since no one will give her by mancipation?
pairs.answer_en: At the buyer's own risk, without mancipation (no warranty of title).
pairs.derivation: The legal trap: a freeborn person cannot lawfully be conveyed by mancipatio, so she is sold sine mancipio at the buyer's risk, which snares Dordalus. Anchored to the play; the terms are supported verbatim (suo periclo is emat... mancipio neque... dabit). Roman law of sale (mancipatio, warranty).

pairs.source_text: DOR. Quid nomen tibist? ... VIR. Lucridi nomen in patria fuit.
pairs.question: Quod nomen sibi ficta virgo in Persa Plauti indit, cum a Dordalo lenone rogatur?
pairs.question_en: What name does the disguised maiden give herself in Plautus' Persa when asked by the pimp Dordalus?
pairs.derivation: Coached for the trick, the girl calls herself Lucris ('Profit'), a name Toxilus hails as a good omen for a greedy leno. Anchored to the play; one-name answer supported verbatim (Lucridi nomen in patria fuit).

pairs.source_text: SAG. Tuo periclo sexaginta haec dabitur argenti minis. DOR. Toxile, quid ago? ... D. Habeto.
pairs.question: Quot argenti minis Dordalus leno virginem captivam in Persa Plauti emit?
pairs.question_en: For how many silver minae does the pimp Dordalus buy the captive maiden in Plautus' Persa?
pairs.derivation: After bargaining down from a hundred, Dordalus buys the girl for sixty silver minae, at his own risk. Anchored to Dordalus + the play; single-number answer supported verbatim (sexaginta... argenti minis... Habeto). Currency realia.

pairs.source_text: sed has tabellas, Paegnium, ipsi Lemniseleni fac des et quae iussi nuntiato.
pairs.question: Quod nomen habet meretrix quam servus Toxilus in Persa Plauti amat et manu mittendam curat?
pairs.question_en: What is the name of the courtesan whom the slave Toxilus loves and arranges to have freed in Plautus' Persa?
pairs.derivation: Toxilus' beloved, for whose freedom the whole intrigue is mounted, is named Lemniselenis. Anchored to Toxilus + the play; one-name answer supported verbatim (ipsi Lemniseleni fac des).

pairs.source_text: SAG. Ita sunt Persarum mores, longa nomina, contortiplicata habemus.
pairs.question: Qualia esse Persarum nomina Sagaristio, Persam simulans, in Persa Plauti affirmat?
pairs.question_en: What sort of names does Sagaristio, playing the Persian, claim the Persians have in Plautus' Persa?
pairs.derivation: The mock-Persian stereotype: Persians have long, twisted-up names (Sagaristio invents an absurdly long one). Anchored to the play; short answer supported verbatim (Persarum mores, longa nomina, contortiplicata). Culturally salient ethnic caricature.

pairs.source_text: cuiquam mortali libero auris atteram, qui hic commercaris civis homines liberos?
pairs.question: Quod scelus Dordalo lenoni in Persa Plauti obicitur, cum eum Saturio in ius rapit?
pairs.question_en: What crime is charged against the pimp Dordalus in Plautus' Persa, when Saturio hauls him to court?
pairs.answer_en: That he traffics in free citizens.
pairs.derivation: The leno's offense, the crux of the play's justice: he buys and sells freeborn citizens. Anchored to Dordalus + the play; answer supported verbatim (qui hic commercaris civis homines liberos). Roman ius against enslaving the freeborn.

pairs.source_text: DOR. Nonne antestaris? SAT. Tuan ego causa, carnufex, cuiquam mortali libero auris atteram,
pairs.question: Quam corporis partem tangebat qui alium ad testimonium antestabatur, ut ex Persa Plauti apparet?
pairs.question_en: Which part of the body did one touch when calling someone to witness (antestari) a summons, as appears from Plautus' Persa?
pairs.derivation: Roman legal ritual: to make someone a witness to an in ius vocatio one touched his ear (antestari). Anchored to the play; one-word answer supported by the text (antestaris... auris atteram). Culturally salient bit of Roman procedure.
